activity.title: I never thought I’d make a post like this on LinkedIn, but I believe it’s time to make it public. A few days ago, my Microsoft offer for a Summer 2026 Software Engineering Internship was rescinded. I received an email from my recruiter stating that, since I am affected by the latest travel ban and the presidential proclamation banning (basically) all Iranians from obtaining any type of visa, my eligibility to apply for work authorization in the U.S. was automatically revoked, and therefore my offer was automatically rescinded. In my initial reply, I asked about alternative work opportunities, either remotely from Canada or from a Canadian office (since I am fully eligible to permanently live and work in Canada), but these questions were not addressed in their response, which appeared to be a general template. Something similar happened to me last year with AMD. One week before the start date of my work term, I received a phone call from AMD telling me that, since my most recent citizenship is Iranian, I could not receive an export control license to begin working. They then told me to look for alternative work opportunities one week before my start date. My original recruiter later kindly sent me a heartfelt email acknowledging the hard situation, explaining how this was outside their control. This is not a political rant, as much as I want it to be. I feel deeply hurt, and I wish all my hardworking and talented Iranian fellows, friends, and classmates peace, patience, success, and equal opportunities. I’m sharing this to try to save my career and reach out to my network to kindly ask for help. If you know of any opportunities for Summer 2026 that do not require a US-based work visa or an export license, I would truly appreciate it if you could share them with me, either in the comments so others can benefit as well, or by DM or reaching me at kiarash.sotoudeh@mail.utoronto.ca . Wishing everybody the very best and a great 2026, Kiarash ...more

“No man ever steps in the same river twice” Well I did. Here’s what my 2 internships at HubSpot taught me about B2B sales: Jk but here’s some cool SWE stuff I did: 🚀 Drove development of an internal components editor now standardized across teams for debugging, testing, and sharing sandbox (I even got suggested to use my own tool in my second time around!) ⚡DRI for a processor-switching project that played a big part in meeting Commerce’s $X0 Millions revenue goal 🔄Led migration from CodeMirror → Monaco (the editor under the hood of VS Code) 📚Made a knowledge-sharing doc to help onboard new engineers 🥀Won fall cohort’s “funniest person award” 🐀Saw an ungodly number of rats in Boston (the exposure therapy I didn’t ask for 💔) Though I didn’t learn much about B2B sales, I did take away some valuable lessons about my career in tech: - Success looks different on every team, what works for 1 might not work for another, so it’s important to recognize which skills matter most in each environment - Make sure you fully understand a problem before solving it, and come up with several possible solutions with tradeoffs before picking one to implement. Coding should be the easiest step. So no I didn’t really “step in the same river twice” because the truth is, the river changes and so do we. I’m not the same engineer I was when I started. I’ve grown in technical depth, learned how I work best, and discovered what excites me most about building in tech. I’m incredibly grateful for the experience, proud of the impact I made, and more excited than ever to take these lessons into my next adventures 👀🚀 ...more

We haven't shared much about our Co-Ops so far, so here's a story from Tran Bui , our Fall Software Engineering Co-Op 🤩 "Hi everyone! My name is Tran Bui, and I’m currently a #SoftwareEngineering Co-op on HubSpot 's Frontend Infra Core team. One of my main contributions during my time here has been working on the Foundations Editor, an internal tool that empowers HubSpot frontend developers to efficiently create and customize sections in our design tools. This project has allowed me to contribute to something that impacts developers across teams, and it’s been so rewarding to see it in action! 🤔 Why did I choose HubSpot? As a minority in tech, I’ve always valued inclusivity, and HubSpot walks the talk. From women in leadership to honoring pronouns and celebrating people from diverse backgrounds, the culture here is unmatched. I appreciate HubSpot’s commitment to team autonomy and keeping teams small to stay fast and productive. I also love the no-blame culture where mistakes aren’t about pointing fingers but about collectively finding solutions to prevent future issues. 💡 Advice for maintaining mental health during an internship: I think it really comes down to having a balance -- pick up hobbies, build a fulfilling life outside of work and a strong support system of friends and family. Communication is another big one: regularly check in with your team about expectations and feedback. This not only helps you grow but also keeps self-doubt in check with clear, actionable paths forward instead of overthinking. This pic is from our Co-ops #Cambridge office visit. We had so much fun and HubSpot is definitely where you want to be if you want to grow your professional network because there are so many smart (and fun) people here! I’m super grateful for my time at HubSpot and the chance to learn from so many talented engineers and be in a work culture where everyone roots for my success. Feel free to reach out if you’re curious about my journey or have questions about HubSpot!" ...more ...more

Mom, I made it! Growing up in Long Xuyen, a little town in Vietnam where most people’s goal was to study in Ho Chi Minh City let alone studying abroad, I always envied the kids from big cities and asked my mom why can’t we just move there? Why do they have easy access so many exclusive resources that I needed to work so hard for? But now that I think about it, I realize that it was a blessing in disguise — the lack of resources trained me to be a resilient go-getter. It has been a wild journey. You can never convince little me that I would one day study in the US (because what do you mean I now use the English that I learned from youtube to put me through advanced technical college courses), and major in CS even though I have 0 coding skills before college, but still decided to go for it anyway because I always have faith that I can do whatever I put my mind to. So, on behalf of 14 year old me, I’m proud to announce that I’ve accepted an offer to be a Software Engineer Intern at Bank of America for Summer 2024. Thank you so much to Michelle Boston for seeing my potential, and to many interviewers and recruiters that I’ve had a chance to talk to for so many fulfilling conversations that I did not expect from a convention setting. Thank you to my roomate Linda Nguyen for answering all my convention related questions, Shovan Shakya and Danny Sor for doing mock interviews with me, Riya George Zhanna Sergeeva Desaiae De Four for being the best convention buddies I could ever ask for. And thank you to all the friends that I made along the way, you know who you are, for being so supportive and making the convention so unforgettable. I am extremely grateful for how far I’ve come, and excited to see what I can do next! ...more

We pivoted 8 times in 16 months before Mintlify became Mintlify. I shared some of that story with a16z speedrun 's current cohort this week, and a few of the lessons I wish someone had told me earlier in my journey: 1. There's no mistaking PMF if you have it. If you're asking yourself whether you have it, you don't. 2. Explosive early traction is not necessarily PMF. We scaled one product to 10,000+ users, then watched everyone stop using it. Growth can be a signal, but without strong retention, it's often a false positive. 3. It's an advantage to pivot within the same problem space. Your learnings, potential customers, and founder market fit compound. 4. PMF is a moving target. Technology changes, competitors change, the world changes. The goal isn't to find PMF once. It's to continually evolve alongside the market. 5. At the earliest stage, giving up is the only way to fail. Almost every bad thing that could have happened, happened and we'd survive it. We knew that quitting will end the journey no matter what. That mentality carried us through the hardest stretches. To the early stage founders still grinding through your own pivots right now, know that everyone you look up to was once exactly where you are. Keep going.

It took me 72 tries and 3 years to solve this leetcode question Since May 2023, "Sum of Total Strength of Wizards" has been my arch nemesis question. The first two weeks I tried 53 times but could never get past a time limit error. Over the next 2 years I attempted it on and off, but never with any success. I randomly came across this question again last week, but this time I saw the idea immediately. It was simple: We need to be able to add arithmetic progressions to an array, efficiently. For instance [+3, +8, +13, +18, ...]. To do this, I used a lazy propagation arithmetic progression segment tree. I must have learned this technique some time in between my prior attempts and now. I think it was from the "Polynomial Queries" problem on CSES which uses the same subroutine. Being able to easily solve questions you couldn't in the past is a 10/10 feeling. Hopefully future Ishaan finds today's struggle problems easy too 😆

I was at YC AI SUS last year. Now I’m back, this time in Y Combinator with InsForge If you’re going to AI SUS and want to maximize your chances of getting into YC, here are a few things I’d do differently: 1. Network with your peers, but choose wisely. There are tons of afterparties and side events. You can’t go to everything. Spend time with founders you can actually learn from, build with, and stay connected with after the event. You can meet a lot of yc founders along the way 👀 2. Talk to YC partners. This is one of the rare chances to get direct advice from YC partners. Use it. Last year, I pitched our idea to Aaron Epstein and got his feedback. Don’t be afraid to walk up, introduce yourself, and talk about what you’re building. 3. Leave with concrete action items. This isn’t university. Don’t just sit through lectures, take notes, and go home. Build something. Talk to users. Try products from YC startups. Figure out what you can execute on immediately. The biggest value of AI SUS isn’t what happens on stage. It’s what you do with the people, feedback, and opportunities around you.

200 hards to go! 🙂 I solved 4 today: 2713. Maximum Strictly Increasing Cells in a Matrix: Find the longest increasing path in a grid where we can travel to any cell in our row or column. I used bottom up DP, O(n*m*log(m*n)) because of sorting 460. LFU Cache: Support the ability to get, add, and update keys/values in a data structure. We evict by least-frequently used key if we exceed the capacity. All operations must be O(1) amortized. I did all operations in O(1) worst case using a somewhat cursed doubly linked list 1505. Minimum Possible Integer After at Most K Adjacent Swaps On Digits: Given a number of length <= 3e4, and K <= 1e9 operations where we can swap two adjacent digits, find the minimum number we can make with at most K swaps. I did an O(10*n*log(n)) solution with a sorted container, can also do a seg tree or lazy seg tree, all three are fundamentally different 420. Strong Password Checker: A strong password must have 6-20 characters, a lowercase and uppercase letter, a digit, and no repeating characters of length 3. Given a weak password, find the min # of operations (insert, delete, replace) to make it strong. I did casework based on the length of the weak password. The 6-20 case was slightly annoying.

Today, I am excited to share that Rivo has raised $3.1M in total funding, including a $2.7M seed round, to build the AI layer for personal finance, starting with automated cash management. Rivo was born from a frustrating personal experience. My former wealth manager had left my hard-earned money earning 0% because he needed "explicit instructions" before moving it, while continuing to charge a 0.65% management fee. That experience made me realize there had to be a better way to manage idle cash. The more I looked into it, the more I realized this wasn't just my problem. U.S. households hold nearly $6 trillion in transaction accounts, much of it earning close to nothing. Not because people don't care, but because they are busy, and the system was designed to profit from that. That's why we built Rivo. It connects to your existing bank account, automatically puts your idle cash to work, and brings it back before bills are due. You keep your bank and never have to manually transfer money. I am incredibly fortunate to be building this alongside an exceptional team. Vince Maniago , our Head of Product, helped build and scale Mint and Personal Capital. Raj Kiran, our CTO, previously built foundation models at Microsoft and Krutrim. Shruti Sharma , our Head of Risk and Compliance, brings deep experience across Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, and LinkedIn. And Sathya Kasturi, Anirudh Vasudevan , Prince Sinha and Abhishek Mishra, who have built this with us since the beginning. I am also grateful to have the support of our amazing investors: South Park Commons , Wisdom Ventures , Script Capital , 645 Ventures , 20VC , and Jag Duggal (former CPO at Nubank). Thank you for believing in our vision. Finally, this milestone wouldn't have been possible without our early beta users who trusted us from day one. And today isn't just about the funding. We are officially open to the public. If you have ever felt like your money should be working harder without creating more work for you, we would love for you to check us out. This Week in Fintech featured our funding announcement (link in comments).
